Arta Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Arta, Greece

Demolished. Benjamin of Tudela recorded a Jewish community in Arta in the 12th century, persisting through the 14th-15th centuries; it reached its spiritual and financial peak in the 16th century as the region's leading community, numbering about 1,800 Romaniot Jews and refugees divided into four distinct congregations, each with its own synagogue. Rabbis actively mediated congregational disputes, though some financial and personal conflicts reached Muslim courts; notable 16th-17th century figure Rabbi Shemuel Kalai, author of Mishpetei Shemuel, was a respected halakhic authority. 18th-century emigration to the Land of Israel followed; by Greek annexation in 1881, only one synagogue remained, with many emigrating mostly to North America. Population reached about 800 by the century's start with a Jewish school and new synagogue, settling at 384 by 1940. About 90% of the community perished in the camps during the 1940s; postwar reestablishment attempts ultimately failed, with the community formally dissolved by government order in 1959 - nothing remains of Arta's Jewish community today. This cemetery's exact founding is unknown, likely 14th-15th century, though it probably began regular operation in the 16th century.
